---
title: "Diagnostics beside the benchmark"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 96, out.width = "100%")
```

The benchmark scores each model on Overlap, Structure and
Behaviour. Three diagnostics look at failures those columns can miss. They
come from recent studies of synthetic survey respondents, and they do not
change the benchmark score:

- `synthetic_construct()`: Do the scales hold together and relate to each
  other as they do in real people?
- `respondent_coverage()`: Does every real person have a synthetic
  look-alike, and do synthetic respondents stay inside the real data?
- `synthetic_copula()` and `authenticity_benchmark(copula = TRUE)`: How
  does a generator with no language model do?

The diagnostics compare models and support decisions about them. They do not
show that synthetic data can replace a field test.

## The data

All 240 HEXACO items for Canada, with three attempts per model:

```{r}
library(synthcheck)

real <- hexaco_real[hexaco_real$country == "Canada", ]
ca <- hexaco_llm[hexaco_llm$country == "Canada" & hexaco_llm$attempt <= 3, ]
synthetic <- as_synthetic_list(ca, items = hexaco_items$item)
```

## Construct structure

Structure averages over every pair of items, which is 28,680 pairs for 240
items. A model can do well there and still blur the six traits together, or
make every scale too coherent. `synthetic_construct()` makes three checks for
each scale and model:

- **Trait correlations:** `trait_cor_gap` is the mean absolute difference
  between the synthetic and the real correlations among the scale scores.
- **Reliability:** `alpha_gap` is the synthetic minus the real Cronbach's
  alpha. Above 0 means the items hang together more tightly than in real
  people. That is the "too coherent" pattern, not a better result.
- **Loadings:** `phi` is Tucker's congruence between the synthetic and the
  real one-factor loadings of each scale. Loadings of similar size give a
  high `phi` by chance, so each value is compared with a permutation null
  (`phi_null`). `rejects` is the share of scales whose `phi` is above
  chance.

```{r}
cs <- synthetic_construct(synthetic, real, hexaco_items, n_perm = 100, n_splits = 10)
cs
```

The "Real (second sample)" row shows how big the gaps are from sampling
noise alone. The correlations between traits show the largest differences:

```{r, fig.width = 10}
gg_construct(cs, "cor")
```

Red means two traits relate less strongly than in real people, blue more
strongly. `gg_construct(cs)` shows alpha per scale on the same colour scale.

## Respondent coverage

Overlap looks at scale scores one scale at a time. `respondent_coverage()`
treats each respondent as one point, the keyed answers to all items, and
measures distances to the nearest neighbour (Kumagae & Kaneko, 2026):

- **RCG:** How far real people are from the nearest synthetic respondent.
  Above 1 means some real people have no synthetic look-alike.
- **OSR:** How far synthetic respondents are from the nearest real person.
  Above 1 means some synthetic respondents sit outside the real data.

Both ratios are scaled by the distance between real people, so a second
sample of real people gives about 1 on both.

```{r}
rc <- respondent_coverage(synthetic, real, hexaco_items, n_draws = 3)
rc
```

```{r, fig.height = 5}
gg_respondent_coverage(rc)
```

Every model has RCG above 1 and OSR below 1, which is the "contraction"
pattern. Synthetic respondents stay close to some real people, but they
leave others uncovered. `pattern` names it once RCG is more than `tol`
(0.1 by default) above 1, so the models closest to 1 are still labelled
"Human-like". Synthetic respondents that were simply noisy would show up as
"off-support", with both ratios above 1.

## A copula reference row

`synthetic_copula()` draws respondents from a Gaussian copula of the real
data. It keeps each item's answer distribution and the correlations between
items, and nothing else. With `copula = TRUE`, the benchmark adds it as a
row:

```{r}
items <- hexaco_items[hexaco_items$trait %in% c("H", "C"), ]
bm <- authenticity_benchmark(synthetic, real, items, fit_scales = character(0),
                             n_splits = 10, n_floor = 10, copula = TRUE)
bm$table[, c("model", "reference", "score", "overlap", "structure", "behaviour")]
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.8}
gg_benchmark(bm)
```

A model below the copula row does no better than this generator. Keep in
mind that the copula is fitted to the real data it is compared with. That
makes it an in-sample reference rather than a competitor, and it is why its
Overlap and Structure can go above 100. You can also use its respondents on
their own:

```{r}
cop <- synthetic_copula(real, n = 500, items = hexaco_items, attempts = 2)
dim(cop[[1]])
```

## References

- Chidichimo, E., Jung, M. J., Wallis, F. P. S., & He, J. K. (2026).
  Artificial Societies Benchmark: A validation framework for synthetic
  research. [arXiv:2609.30030](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.30030).
- Kumagae, Y., & Kaneko, M. (2026). Silicon samples match the answers but
  not the respondents. [arXiv:2610.30900](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30900).
- Lukauskas, M., & Šarkauskaitė, V. (2026). Plausible but not valid: A
  psychometric audit of LLMs as synthetic survey respondents.
  [arXiv:2608.14606](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14606).
